newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia issues new warning against NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia issues new warning against NATO expansion.

text.p: Russia on Friday issued another warning on NATO expansion, with the foreign minister saying that if the alliance ignores Russian security concerns, Moscow may have to seriously rethink its external policy.

It was the latest in a series of tough statements from Moscow aimed at winning concessions from the West before NATO meets in July to consider inviting several former Soviet allies in central and eastern Europe to join the western alliance.

"If Russia's concerns are not taken into account, under these conditions we would be forced to think of very serious changes, including in the conduct of foreign relations," Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told journalists.

Primakov, speaking after addressing a closed session of parliament on NATO and Russian foreign policy, appeared to be trying to present a convincing strategy on NATO expansion, although he did not say what policy changes he had in mind.

He outlined three possible outcomes of the West's intention to issue invitations to former Warsaw Pact members. The third variant, he said, was that NATO did not pay any attention to Russian concerns, forcing Moscow to respond.
The first possible outcome was that the 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation would decide against accepting new members, but Primakov said that this "was not likely".
The second possibility was a serious effort by NATO members to consider Russia's concerns on the alliance's expansion -- which Russian officials say could threaten Moscow's security.
"It is to this end that we are striving," Primakov said. "It is precisely because of this that we have started consultations and negotiations with NATO."

Although the country's top military brass openly admit that Russia's armed forces are in shambles, officials have recently warned that expansion of the once-rival NATO could force them to rebuild their arsenal.

"NATO expansion will force Russia to change its national security doctrine and ... increase military spending," Gennady Seleznyov, the speaker of Russia's State Duma told Polish parliamentarians earlier this week.
With a sustained depression gripping its economy, it is unclear if Russia could make good on such threats.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday that there had been at times "ludicrous" comments from some voices in Russia about NATO and added: "No one, and I mean no one, will have a veto over which countries can join."
But, speaking at a news conference after a summit meeting with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, he said efforts should be made to address Russian concerns about NATO expansion.
Earlier this week, Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais said Moscow was seeking guarantees that NATO troops and nuclear weapons would not be moved near Russia's borders.

NATO expansion is expected to be a key topic at a planned summit meeting next month between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton. U.S. officials say it is expected to be held in Helsinki.
During talks with Yeltsin in Moscow last Sunday, French President Jacques Chirac also proposed a summit in France to discuss details of NATO's expansion.

Diplomats in Paris said that under the proposal, leaders of the United States, Russia, France, Germany and Britain would meet in April to establish the broad lines of a deal on future European security to enable Moscow to accept NATO enlargement.
The U.S. State Department has virtually ruled out the idea, which is backed by Germany, saying it had not received any such proposal and did not expect one would be forthcoming.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana held talks last month with Primakov and the two are scheduled to meet again in Brussels on February 23.
